lead: Friction takes a share of the power the burning fuel produces at every load, and at idle it takes nearly all of it. The lubrication system exists to keep that share small: it stores oil, cleans it, pumps it at the right pressure and delivers it to every sliding pair, rings, bearings and valve gear. This chapter lists where friction comes from, explains how an oil film carries load, and describes the circuits (mist, splash, pressure feed, wet sump and dry sump) that place oil on the right surface at the right moment.
prereq: You need: the rings, bearings and crank train from engine components, and indicated and brake power from engine testing and performance.

blocks.text: Lubrication has more jobs than reducing friction. An engine oil must:

items: Reduce friction and wear between sliding parts.
Cool: oil carries heat away from the piston underside, bearings and turbo shaft.
Seal: the film between rings and liner helps hold compression.
Clean: oil washes wear debris and soot to the filter.
Cushion shock loads in the bearings, and protect metal against rust and acids.

blocks.text: Not all the power that the burning charge pushes onto the piston reaches the flywheel. Some is spent overcoming friction between moving parts, and some is spent pushing gas in and out of the cylinder. Together they form the friction power, FP. It is defined as the gap between the power developed inside the cylinder and the power delivered at the crankshaft.

blocks.where: FP is friction power (kW); IP is indicated power, the power developed on the piston (kW); BP is brake power, the power measured at the crankshaft (kW).

blocks.text: Rubbing friction comes from four places. Piston rings press on the cylinder wall and carry the gas load; the skirt rubs sideways as the rod swings. Main and big-end bearings shear their oil film. The valve train — cam, tappets, pushrods, rockers — rubs on every cycle. Pumping loss is separate work: pulling air past a nearly closed throttle and pushing exhaust out. At light load in an SI engine, pumping loss grows large.

Parameters that influence friction: engine speed (friction rises roughly with speed), load (ring pressure rises with cylinder pressure), oil viscosity and its temperature, bore-to-stroke ratio, number of rings, and surface finish. Two quantities summarise the loss: a ratio, the mechanical efficiency, and a pressure, the friction mean effective pressure. Because friction power changes little with load at a fixed speed, mechanical efficiency is highest at full load (often 80 to 90 percent) and falls to zero at idle, where all the indicated power is spent on friction.

blocks.where: η<sub>m</sub> is mechanical efficiency (no unit, often written as a percentage); BP is brake power (kW); IP is indicated power (kW).

fmep is friction mean effective pressure (Pa or bar), a definition only; FP is friction power (W); V<sub>d</sub> is total swept volume (m³); N is speed (rev/min); N/120 is the number of cycles each cylinder completes per second in a four-stroke engine; with V<sub>d</sub> taken as the swept volume of all cylinders together, the product is the swept volume handled per second by the whole engine.

sections.h3: How an oil film carries load

blocks.text: An oil film carries load in three ways, and a running engine passes through all three.

Hydrodynamic lubrication. The journal turns inside the bearing with a small clearance. Viscous drag pulls oil into the narrowing gap ahead of the closest point. That oil cannot escape fast enough, so its pressure rises and forms a wedge, and the journal floats on the wedge. Metal never touches metal. This needs enough speed, enough viscosity and the correct clearance.

Boundary lubrication. The film is a few molecules thick, held on the surface by the oil's own polarity. Load is carried by surface contact, not by fluid pressure, so wear is real. Mixed lubrication lies between boundary and hydrodynamic.

At start-up the shaft rests on the bearing and only a boundary film exists until the pump builds pressure and speed rises. Those first seconds cause most bearing wear, which is why oil must still flow on a cold morning; viscosity behaviour is covered in Lubricants: properties and additives.

sections.h3: Lubrication methods: mist, splash and pressure feed

blocks.text: Systems are classified by how the oil reaches the surface.

items: Mist (petroil): oil is mixed into the petrol at 2 to 5 percent of the petrol volume (1:50 to 1:20). The fuel-air-oil mist wets the bearings and cylinder, and the rest burns.
Splash: a dipper on the big end scoops oil from a trough and throws it around the crankcase.
Pressure feed: a pump sends oil through drillings to the bearings, and the overflow splashes the walls and valve gear.

blocks.text: Mist lubrication suits two-strokes, which have no sump, and works at any tilt angle. It is cheap, but it fouls spark plugs and smokes. A four-stroke cannot use it: its oil must stay in a sump and be used again, and its crankcase never carries the fuel mixture, so there is no mist to carry the oil.

Splash lubrication is simple and served small stationary engines and old motorcycles. The oil level is critical: too low starves the dipper, too high makes the oil froth. Pressure feed is used on almost all car and truck engines, usually combined with splash for the cylinder walls.

sections.h3: Wet sump and dry sump circuits

blocks.text: A wet sump engine keeps its oil in a pan under the crankcase. Oil flows from the sump through a strainer to the pump, then to the filter, along the main gallery to the bearings, and drains back by gravity.

Each part has a job. The strainer is coarse mesh that stops large debris before the pump. The pump is usually a gear or rotor type driven from the crankshaft. A relief valve beside the pump opens at a set pressure and returns surplus oil to the sump, so the filter and hoses survive cold thick oil. The filter carries a bypass that opens if it clogs. The main gallery is a drilled passage along the block feeding the main bearings, from which drillings lead to the big ends, cam and rockers.

A dry sump engine keeps oil in a separate tank. A scavenge pump pulls oil from a shallow pan into the tank, and a pressure pump feeds the engine from the tank. It costs more and adds plumbing, but oil cannot surge away from the pick-up in a hard corner, the engine can sit lower, and the tank holds more oil that cools better. Racing cars, aircraft and some heavy diesels use it.

examples.question: A 1.6 litre four-cylinder four-stroke engine is motored at 3000 rev/min with the fuel cut off, and the dynamometer reads a torque of 24 N·m. In a firing test at the same speed the indicated power is 30 kW. Find the friction power, the brake power, the mechanical efficiency and the friction mean effective pressure.
steps: While motoring, no fuel burns, so the torque the dynamometer absorbs is the torque needed to overcome friction plus pumping. Speed N = 3000 rev/min, torque T = 24 N·m.
Brake power BP = IP − FP = 30 − 7.54 = 22.46 kW.
Mechanical efficiency η<sub>m</sub> = BP / IP = 22.46 / 30 = 0.7487, that is 74.9 percent.

fmep = FP ÷ (V<sub>d</sub> × N/120) = 7540 W ÷ (1.6 × 10⁻³ m³ × 3000/120 s⁻¹) = 7540 ÷ 0.040 = 188 500 Pa ≈ 1.89 bar. This is the pressure that, acting on the pistons, would do just the friction and pumping work.
examples.answer: Friction power 7.54 kW, brake power 22.46 kW, mechanical efficiency 74.9 percent, fmep about 1.89 bar.

traps: Mechanical efficiency is brake power divided by indicated power, never the other way round. A value above 1 is always a sign of this slip.
Motoring torque gives friction plus pumping loss. It is not pure rubbing friction, so do not call it 'bearing friction only'.
Friction power is IP minus BP. If the question gives brake power and efficiency, first find IP = BP / η<sub>m</sub>, then subtract.
Mist lubrication belongs to crankcase-scavenged two-strokes, where the fuel mixture passes through the crankcase. Writing it for a four-stroke loses marks.

quiz.q: Name the four places where rubbing friction arises in a four-stroke engine, and the separate loss that motoring also measures.
quiz.a: Piston rings, piston skirt, main and big-end bearings, and the valve train (cam, tappets, rockers). Motoring also measures pumping loss, the work of moving gas in and out.

quiz.q: Why does a cold start wear a bearing more than steady hot running?
quiz.a: Cold oil is thick and reaches the bearing slowly, so the journal rests on the surface with only a boundary or mixed film. The full hydrodynamic wedge appears only after oil flow and speed build up.

quiz.q: An engine develops indicated power 45 kW at mechanical efficiency 0.82. Find the brake power and the friction power.
Explain why an oil that is far too viscous can raise friction power.
quiz.a: Thicker oil shears with more resistance inside the bearing and under the rings, so viscous drag adds to friction power. When cold it also reaches distant parts late, delaying the full film. Viscosity should be just enough to keep a complete film.

quiz.q: What is the function of the relief valve in a wet sump system?
quiz.a: It opens at a set pressure and returns excess oil to the sump, so pressure cannot rise enough to damage the filter or hoses, especially with cold thick oil.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a racing car uses a dry sump system.
quiz.a: A separate tank stops oil from surging away from the pick-up during hard cornering, and the shallow pan lets the engine sit lower, lowering the centre of gravity. It also allows a larger oil volume that cools better.

beyond: Production engines now use variable-displacement oil pumps that deliver only the flow speed and load need. Diamond-like carbon coatings on rings and pins, and laser-honed liners, cut rubbing friction without thinner oil. Search for variable displacement oil pump, DLC piston ring coating and friction mean effective pressure breakdown.
